L1964@P45: Jean-Claude Thelen and Stephan Havemann, Met Office, FitzRoy Road, Exeter, UK
L1965@P45: Abstract : The Havemann-Taylor Fast Radiative Transfer Code (HT- FRTC) is based on Principal Components (PCs)
L1966@P45: and allows fast and exact radiance and/or transmittance calculations. It is ideally suited for the simulation of hyperspectral sensors with hundreds or thousands of channels. The HT-FRTC can simulate a full instrument spectrum for any atmosphere and
L1967@P45: surface within a few milliseconds. It works for satellite- based, airborne and ground-based sensors. The code has been applied in
L1968@P45: any part of the spectrum from the short-wave to the long-wave (i.e. infrared plus microwave). It includes the solar and the lunar
L1969@P45: source and can account for the spherical Earth. The HT-FRTC has been incorporated into a one- dimensional variational (1DVar) retrieval system that also works solely in PC space. This keeps the dimensions of the matrices involved small. The solution of
L1970@P45: the full non-linear problem is achieved by an iterative Levenberg-Marquardt minimization procedure. The retrieval state vector
L1971@P45: includes the vertical profiles of atmospheric temperature, water vapour and ozone, and possibly other trace gases as well as the
L1972@P45: surface temperature and surface emissivity / reflectivity (the latter being represented by a set of PCs). For a scattering atmosphere,
L1973@P45: cloud parameters and aerosol parameters have been added to the state vector. The cloud part of the state vector for cirrus cloud
L1974@P45: includes cloud-top pressure, ice water content, cloud fraction and cloud geometrical thickness. For water cloud there is also an
L1975@P45: effective droplet size.

L1983@P45: Abstract : In this study two neural networks were implemented in order to emulate a retrieval model and to estimate the
L1984@P45: sulphur dioxide (SO2) columnar content and plume height from volcanic eruption. ANNs were trained using all IASI channels in
L1985@P45: TIR as inputs, and the corresponding values of SO2 content and height of plume obtained using the Oxford SO2 retrievals as target
L1986@P45: outputs. The retrieval is demonstrated for the eruption of the Eyjafjallajökull volcano (Iceland) occured in 2010 and to three IASI
L1987@P45: images of the Grímsvötn volcanic eruption that occurred in May 2011, in order to evaluate the networks for a different eruption.
L1988@P45: The results of validation, both for Eyjafjallajökull and Grímsvötn independent datasets, provided RMSE values between neural
L1989@P45: network outputs and targets lower than 20 DU for SO2 total column and 200 mb for plume height, therefore demonstrating the
L1990@P45: feasibility to estimate SO2 values using a neural network approach, and its importance in near real time monitoring activities, owing to its fast application. Concerning the validation carried out with neural networks on images from the Grímsvötn eruption,
L1991@P45: the RMSE of the outputs remained lower than the Standard Deviation (STD) of targets, and the neural network underestimated
L1992@P45: retrieval only where target outputs showed different statistics than those used during the training phase.

L2003@P46: Abstract : X-ray diffraction is a powerful technique to provide information on the molecular structure of samples. Energy dispersive X-ray diffraction (EDXRD) spectra are classically measured at one single fixed scattering angle using a polychromatic X- ray source and a spectroscopic detector. In order to remove system blurring and restore material proper information,
L2004@P46: inversion of the EDXRD spectra is required. This paper proposes to combine EDXRD spectra at different scattering angles to
L2005@P46: improve reconstruction results. To quantify the improvements, detective quantum efficiency (DQE) calculations are used, which
L2006@P46: allow to compare the performance of mono- and multi-angle systems, are used. We present a reconstruction method based on
L2007@P46: multi-angle EDXRD spectra. The algorithm was tested on simulated salt (NaCl) spectra. Finally, advantages of multi-angle over
L2008@P46: mono-angle spectra are discussed.

L2026@P46: Abstract : The physical basis of rock identification is spectral feature. In order to remove the rock spectrum noise, the
L2027@P46: discrete wavelet transform (DWT) was used to deal with the spectra of 13 rock samples of metamorphic rocks collected in mineral
L2028@P46: reservation region. The Biorthogonal 4.4 wavelet of the scale of decomposition was selected was selected as the mother wavelet
L2029@P46: to smooth the spectra and highlight features of absorption. By correspondence analyzing (CA) spectra normalized by DWT, we
L2030@P46: find that the rock spectra were classified into three clusters through analyzing two-dimensional image of CA. The first cluster has
L2031@P46: higher reflectivity than other two clusters, because the compound of light-colored minerals, the key to high reflectivity, of the first
L2032@P46: cluster is greater than that that of other two clusters. The second cluster has obvious iron alteration. The third cluster has obvious
L2033@P46: clay alteration. The results of classification, verified by cluster analysis, are better corresponding. The paper provides a physical
L2034@P46: basis for Metamorphic rocks classification and identification by using remote sensing technology.

L2043@P47: Abstract : The hyperspectral remote sensing in the thermal infrared region is being acknowledged as an innovative tool
L2044@P47: for Earth environmental studies and is complimentary to the optical range. The current study focuses on surface mineral content
L2045@P47: mapping using day and night airborne data in the LWIR spectral range over a well known mineralogical site in Israel. The data
L2046@P47: was acquired with the AisaOWL hyperspectral sensor over Ramon crater in the Negev desert in southern Israel. The identification
L2047@P47: of major minerals was enabled by locating similarities in day and night at-sensor radiance spectra. The analysis resulted with the
L2048@P47: classification of quartz, carbonates, gypsum, kaolinite and other silicates according to their observed spectral features in both day
L2049@P47: and night data.

L2051@P47: Virginia E. García Millán, Kian Pakzad, Ulrike Faude, Sebastian Teuwsen and Andreas Müterthies
L2052@P47: EFTAS Fernerkundung, GmbH. Oststrasse, 2-18, 48155, Münster (NRW), Germany
L2053@P47: Abstract : The present research is developed in the frame of the R&D project GMES4Mining, which aims to support
L2054@P47: particular tasks within the different phases of a mining life cycle [1]. During the exploitation and after the closure of the mine,
L2055@P47: environmental and civil impacts may happen, due to changes in the compacting properties of the soil related to mining activities.
L2056@P47: In this paper, we focus in the emergence of flooded areas, due to a subsidence of the ground surface. Above-ground vegetation
L2057@P47: is affected by changes in groundwater’s dynamics; at first trees suffer defoliation and senescence, and after some time, they die.
L2058@P47: Several methods have been tested, to detect changes in spectral response of forests in a mine area, which are related to imminent
L2059@P47: flooding. ENVI’s Target Detection Tool has been used to estimate the reflectance proportion at pixel level of four targets of interest
L2060@P47: in AISA-Eagle’s data, which are present in flooded areas: water, dead trunks, senescent trees and green stands within water. Five
L2061@P47: target detection’s methods have been tested: Constrained Energy Minimization (CEM), Adaptative Coherence Estimator (ACE),
L2062@P47: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Target-Constrained Interference- Minimized Filter (TCIMF) and Mixture Tuned Matched Filtering (MTMF).
L2063@P47: POSSIBILITIES FOR THE STUDY OF THE NLTE EFFECT ON ATMOSPHERIC CO2 SPECTRAL SIGNATURES INDUCED BY A BLUE JET USING AN INFRARED SPECTRO- IMAGER EMBEDDED IN A STRATOSPHERIC BALLOON.

L2066@P47: F. Duruisseau, N. Huret, Laboratoire de Physique et Chimie de l’Environnement, CNRS and Université d’Orléans, Orléans, France
L2067@P47: Abstract : HALESIS (High Altitude Luminous Events Studied by Infrared Spectro-imagery) is an innovative project
L2068@P47: based on hyperspectral imagery. The purpose of this experience is to measure the atmospheric perturbation in the minutes following the occurrence of Transient Luminous Events (TLEs) from a stratospheric balloon in the altitude range of 20 to 40 km. The
L2069@P47: first part of the study has been dedicated to establish the project feasibility. To do that, we have simulated spectral perturbations
L2070@P47: induced by an isolated blue jet. Simulations have been performed using the line by line radiative transfer model LBLRM taking
L2071@P47: into account the Non Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium. The case of the estimation of the CO2 infrared signature that could be
L2072@P47: the result of a single blue jet occurrence is presented.
L2073@P47: Then, the estimated spectral signatures have been confronted with the technical capabilities of different kinds of hyperspectral imagers. The study has demonstrated the feasibility of the project, but it has also pointed to the challenges to build
L2074@P47: perfectly adapted instrument.

L2093@P48: Abstract : To acquire accurate, real-time hyperspectral images with high spatial resolution, we develop two types of lowcost, lightweight Whisk broom hyperspectral sensors that can be loaded onto lightweight unmanned autonomous vehicle (UAV)
L2094@P48: platforms. A system is composed of two Mini- Spectrometers, a polygon mirror, references for sensor calibration, a GPS sensor,
L2095@P48: a data logger and a power supply. The acquisition of images with high spatial resolution is realized by a ground scanning along
L2096@P48: a direction perpendicular to the flight direction based on the polygon mirror. To cope with the unstable illumination condition
L2097@P48: caused by the low-altitude observation, skylight radiation and dark current are acquired in real-time by the scanning structure.
L2098@P48: Another system is composed of 2D optical fiber array connected to eight Mini- Spectrometers and a telephoto lens, a convex lens,
L2099@P48: a micro mirror, a GPS sensor, a data logger and a power supply. The acquisition of images is realized by a ground scanning based
L2100@P48: on the rotation of the micro mirror.

L2106@P48: Abstract : Improving the spectral detail of earth observation imaging from Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS)
L2107@P48: can greatly expand its potential for use in vegetation monitoring and specifically in precision agriculture. Spatially variable interference filters which can be placed very close to the image sensor offer an excellent opportunity for reducing the size, mass and
L2108@P48: complexity of hyperspectral imagers, allowing them to be mounted onboard small RPAS. Recent advances in filter deposition
L2109@P48: techniques allow to directly deposit interference filters on an image sensor. The monolithic integration of optical hyperspectral
L2110@P48: filters on top of a standard CMOS image sensor has been demonstrated by IMEC. Compared to the more conventional deposition
L2111@P48: of filters onto an external glass substrate, this new approach offers advantages in terms of cost, alignment accuracy, straylight , etc..
L2112@P48: A hyperspectral camera prototype compatible with small RPAS has been developed by VITO to demonstrate the potential of LVF-based compact spectral camera’s. Whereas application of the filter technology offers major advantages for RPAS
L2113@P48: systems, it still faces some important challenges. The prototype system specifications need to fit a fixed wing RPAS platform that is
L2114@P48: able to cover several km2 in a single flight with hyperspectral geo-information. It remains challenging to make a sufficiently compact camera system, achieve precise spectral band registration, handle the amount of data to be processed and cope with limited
L2115@P48: integration times possible during acquisition.

L2124@P49: Abstract : Remote sensing is a key tool for precision agriculture applications as it is capable of capturing spatial and
L2125@P49: temporal variations in crop status. However, satellites often have an inadequate spatial resolution for precision agriculture applications. High-resolution Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) imagery can be obtained at flexible dates, but operational costs may limit
L2126@P49: the collection frequency. The current study utilizes data fusion to create a dataset which benefits from the temporal resolution
L2127@P49: of Formosat-2 imagery and the spatial resolution of UAV imagery with the purpose of monitoring crop growth in a potato field.
L2128@P49: The correlation of the Weighted Difference Vegetation Index (WDVI) from fused imagery to measured crop indicators at field
L2129@P49: level and added value of the enhanced spatial and temporal resolution are discussed. The results of the STARFM method were
L2130@P49: restrained by the requirement of same-day base imagery. However, the unmixing-based method provided a high correlation to the
L2131@P49: field data and accurately captured the WDVI temporal variation at field level (r=0.969).

L2133@P49: S.Delalieux, D. Raymaekers and K. Nackaerts, VITO – Teledetection and Earth Observation Processes, Belgium
L2134@P49: E. Honkavaara, Finnish Geodetic Institute, Finland
L2135@P49: J. Soukkamäki, Rikola Ltd., Finland

L2137@P49: Abstract : This preliminary study shows the potential of highly flexible drones and hyperspectral technology to make
L2138@P49: detailed chlorophyll maps of an experimental potato field. A novel, innovative hyperspectral frame camera (Rikola Ltd) was
L2139@P49: employed to gather the spectral information (24 bands) at 5 cm spatial resolution. A first challenge therefore was to set- up a
L2140@P49: dedicated preprocessing chain for the images coming from this novel sensor. Coregistration of the images was successful resulting in an image displacement of only 1-2 pixels. The chlorophyll map created from the Rikola data corresponded well to the field
L2141@P49: measurements. R2 values of 0.70 were found for a linear relation between the averaged field chlorophyll measurements and the
L2142@P49: mean of the (R780- R550)/(R780+R550) index calculated for all vegetated Rikola pixels within an experimental potato cultivar
L2143@P49: plot. These chlorophyll maps which are directly linked to the vegetation status of the crops can be used by the farmer for better
L2144@P49: management decision making.

L2149@P49: Abstract : In the recent years UAV have become an important tool for monitoring and sampling activities in a wide
L2150@P49: range of applications. Last December an UAV was used for the first time to survey the Lusi volcano (Indonesia). The aim was to
L2151@P49: take mud and gas samples, aerial photographs, videos and contact temperature measurements.
L2152@P49: Two different prototypes of remote controlled gas containers were available; in particular one prototype is a real-time

L2161@P50: AN INTRODUCTION TO SPECTRAL GRAPH TECHNIQUES FOR THE ANALYSIS OF HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE DATA
L2162@P50: David Gillisa, Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC, USA
L2163@P50: David Messinger, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, USA
L2164@P50: Abstract : Two of the biggest challenges in analyzing HyperSpectral Image (HSI) data are that, first, the data is very
L2165@P50: high- dimensional, and secondly, by its very nature, HSI contains both spatial and spectral information. In order to make full use
L2166@P50: of this information, models and algorithms should incorporate both aspects of the data; unfortunately, this is a decidedly nontrivial problem. In recent years, spectral graph theory (including manifold learning) has proven to be a very successful technique
L2167@P50: for analyzing high-dimensional data sets. Given the highly abstract nature of graphs, many of these techniques are easily applied
L2168@P50: to HSI data; moreover, by carefully choosing how the graph is constructed, both the spatial and spectral nature of the data can be
L2169@P50: included in the model. In this note, we present a general background overview of spectral graph theory, with an emphasis on how
L2170@P50: it can be used to analyze HSI data (in particular, to perform nonlinear dimensionality reduction as well as segmentation and classification). We include examples from real-world data, and also point out some of the issues (such as computational complexity
L2171@P50: and storage requirements) that need to be addressed.
L2172@P50: SPATIAL CONTEXT DRIVEN MANIFOLD LEARNING FOR HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE
L2173@P50: Y. Zhang, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Houston
L2174@P50: H.L. Yang, School of Civil Engineering, Purdue University, US
L2175@P50: D. Lunga, Meraka Institute, Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, South Africa
L2176@P50: S. Prasad, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Houston
L2177@P50: M. Crawford, School of Civil Engineering, Purdue University, US
L2178@P50: Abstract : Manifold learning techniques have been demonstrated to be successful in representing spectral signatures in
L2179@P50: hyperspectral images, which consist of spectral features with very subtle differences and often spatially induced disjoint classes
L2180@P50: whose neighborhood relations are difficult to capture using traditional graph based embedding techniques. Robust parameter
L2181@P50: estimation is a challenge in traditional kernel functions that compute neighborhood graphs e.g finding the optimal number of
L2182@P50: nearest neighbors. We address these challenges by proposing spatial context driven manifold learning methods. Empirically, the
L2183@P50: study reveals that use of spatial contextual information has a bearing on the structure of the graph Laplacian that in turn links
L2184@P50: image pixel observations to their manifold spaces. Further experimental results demonstrate an improvement in the classification
L2185@P50: performance compared to traditional manifold learning methods.
L2186@P50: DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION OF HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGERY WITH SPARSE AND COLLABORATIVE GRAPHS
L2187@P50: Nam Ly, Qian Du, James E. Fowler and Nicolas Younan,
L2188@P50: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Mississippi State University, USA
L2189@P50: Abstract : Hyperspectral image dimensionality reduction with graph-based approaches is considered. With available
L2190@P50: labeled samples, a graph can be formed with these samples by constructing an affinity matrix through their sparse or collaborative
L2191@P50: representations. In addition, sparse or collaborative representation can be done using within-class samples, resulting in blocksparse representation, although within each block the representation can be either sparse or non-sparse (collaborative). The experimental results show that the block-sparse plus within-block-collaborative representation can yield the best performance.

L2198@P51: Abstract : We propose an approach for capturing the signal variability in hyperspectral imagery using the framework
L2199@P51: of the Grassmann manifold. Labeled points from each class are sampled and used to form abstract points on the Grassmannian.
L2200@P51: The resulting points on the Grassmannian have representations as orthonormal matrices and as such do not reside in Euclidean
L2201@P51: space in the usual sense. There are a variety of metrics which allow us to determine a distance matrices that can be used to realize
L2202@P51: the Grassmannian as an embedding in Euclidean space. We illustrate that we can achieve an approximately isometric embedding
L2203@P51: of the Grassmann manifold using the chordal metric while this is not the case with geodesic distances. However, non-isometric
L2204@P51: embeddings generated by using a pseudometric on the Grassmannian lead to the best classification results. We observe that as
L2205@P51: the dimension of the Grassmannian grows, the accuracy of the classification grows to 100% on two illustrative examples. We also
L2206@P51: observe a decrease in classification rates if the dimension of the points on the Grassmannian is too large for the dimension of the
L2207@P51: Euclidean space. We use sparse support vector machines to perform additional model reduction. The resulting classifier selects a
L2208@P51: subset of dimensions of the embedding without loss in classification performance.
L2209@P51: MULTI-FEATURE BASED LABEL PROPAGATION FOR SEMI-SUPERVISED CLASSIFICATION OF HYPERSPECTRAL DATA
L2210@P51: Andong Ma, Faculty of Information Engineering, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China
L2211@P51: Li Ma, Faculty of Mechanical and Electronic Information Engineering, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, China
L2212@P51: Abstract : For hyperspectral remote sensing, some spatial features e.g., texture and morphological feature, have been successfully employed for classification task. In this paper, we investigate the utilization of multiple features in label propagation (LP)
L2213@P51: classifier, attempting to improve the classification accuracy with small size samples. The graph of LP classifier is constructed by
L2214@P51: using multiple features, where each feature calculates a similarity matrix and a composite similarity matrix is obtained via linear
L2215@P51: combination. To weight the importance of each feature in the combination, leave-one- out strategy is applied to obtain a suitable
L2216@P51: weight for each feature. Experimental results on two high resolution hyperspectral data show that the proposed approach obtained
L2217@P51: better classification performance than LP classifier with single spectral feature and LP with equal weighted multi-feature.
